questions.explain: Forgetting max server memory lets SQL Server starve the OS; set it on every instance (total RAM minus OS reserve). The chapter also stresses separating data, log, and tempdb onto different devices — tempdb on the fastest storage — for I/O isolation.
options: SQL Server automatically reserves enough memory for the OS, so no setting is needed.
min server memory is the only setting that matters.
Leave max server memory unset on dedicated servers for best performance.
Set max server memory to total RAM minus an OS reserve on every instance, and separate data, transaction log, and tempdb onto different physical devices.
questions.q: What memory and storage-layout guidance does the chapter give for on-premises SQL Server deployments?

questions.explain: In virtualized environments, hypervisors can reclaim guest memory under pressure (ballooning), forcing buffer pool evictions — so lock the VM's memory reservation and reserve CPU, preventing the database from competing with other VMs for physical resources.
options: It prevents the hypervisor from migrating the VM.
It avoids Transparent Page Sharing corruption.
It stops the hypervisor reclaiming memory from the database VM under pressure, which would force buffer pool evictions and degrade hit ratios.
It reduces the number of vCPUs the VM can use.
questions.q: Why should you lock the memory reservation (and disable memory ballooning) for a database VM?

questions.explain: Azure SQL Database has no SQL Server Agent (Elastic Jobs instead), and several features (Database Mail, linked servers, some DBCC/ system procedures) are unavailable or differ. Managed Instance is nearly fully compatible — Agent, Database Mail, linked servers, CLR — making it the most natural migration target for on-premises workloads.
options: Azure SQL Database has no SQL Server Agent (use Elastic Jobs) and lacks several on-prem features, while Managed Instance is nearly fully compatible with on-premises SQL Server.
Both are identical to on-premises SQL Server in every respect.
Managed Instance has no SQL Server Agent but Azure SQL Database does.
Neither supports BULK INSERT from Azure Blob Storage.
questions.q: What is the key operational difference between Azure SQL Database and Azure SQL Managed Instance for an on-premises SQL Server workload?

questions.explain: Containers are ephemeral and databases are stateful, so the data directory must map to persistent volumes. If the memory limit is set too low, buffer pool plus query memory grants push the container over the limit and trigger an OOM kill — which SQL Server doesn't handle gracefully.
options: They are used only for stateless application tiers.
Persistent volumes hold the data across container restarts; memory limits must be set with full knowledge of max server memory plus grant headroom, because an OOM kill restarts the instance.
Containers cannot run SQL Server at all.
Memory limits have no effect because SQL Server ignores them.
questions.q: What is the core tension in running SQL Server in containers, and what memory-limit caution does the chapter give?

questions.explain: Always On (including distributed AGs) and log shipping span on-premises/cloud cleanly; the gaps are operational — latency, bandwidth, and WAN failover needing careful quorum design so a network partition doesn't take down both sides. Use private links (ExpressRoute/Direct Connect), not public internet, for replication paths.
options: Replication cannot cross deployment boundaries at all.
Use public internet for replication to reduce latency.
Hybrid replication requires rewriting applications.
Always On / distributed AGs and log shipping span the boundary, but you need reliable low-jitter connectivity (ExpressRoute/Direct Connect) and careful WAN quorum design.
questions.q: For a hybrid deployment with the primary on-premises and a replica in Azure, what replication and networking guidance does the chapter give?
